lead: Requirements engineering is the work that turns a need into agreed, testable requirements. It is a loop, not a one-time form: check feasibility, elicit needs, analyse them, write a specification, validate it, and manage every change. The loop exists because needs and constraints move while the project runs. Early checks stop a team from building a system that cannot be paid for, cannot be operated, or cannot be delivered on time. Indian teams use it in fee portals, UPI collections, IRCTC-style bookings and campus systems.
prereq: You need: 2.1 for requirement types and Unit 1 for life-cycle phases.

blocks.text: The process starts with feasibility: a short study that asks whether the project is worth starting. Its output is a feasibility report with a go, no-go or change-scope recommendation.
Elicitation gathers needs from users, sponsors, operators and rule owners. Output: interview notes, workshop records, source documents and a stakeholder list. 2.3 covers how to run it.
Analysis turns raw needs into consistent models and checks conflicts. Output: use cases, class models, data flow diagrams and a ranked list of non-functional targets. Links: 2.6, 2.7, 2.8.
Specification writes the agreed requirements in the SRS. Output: a reviewed document. 2.5 gives its shape.
Validation checks that the written requirements are the right ones. Output: review records, testable acceptance checks and defects sent back. 2.4 covers validation and change control.

Management runs beside every stage: it keeps versions, change requests, trace links and decisions visible. Some syllabi call the first five stages 'requirements development' and the side activity 'requirements management'.
Validation can send work back to elicitation or analysis; that feedback arrow is the loop.

Feasibility asks whether a project can be done under its constraints. It is not a full business case: it does not price every alternative or forecast every year. It is a short, evidence-based screen before spending heavily.

items: Technical: can the team build it with known technology, skills and load? Compute peak rates, data volume and integration limits.
Economic: do benefits exceed costs? Use cost-benefit, payback and net benefit.
Legal: does it follow laws, contracts, audit rules, data protection and payment rules?
Operational: will users run it in real work? Check training, receipts, support, language and accessibility.
Schedule: can the required scope be delivered by the needed date? List the minimum scope and its risks.

blocks.text: annual net benefit = annual savings − annual operating cost − (one-time cost ÷ life in years); payback = one-time cost ÷ (annual savings − annual operating cost)
blocks.where: annual savings is the money saved each year; annual operating cost is gateway, SMS, support and maintenance; one-time cost is the initial build and purchase; life in years is the period over which that cost is spread; payback is the time to recover the initial cost from annual cash saving.

blocks.text: Use measured numbers, not wishes. A portal that saves clerk overtime but adds gateway fees can look good in a demo and weak in a ledger.
A project can pass one check and fail another. Report each axis separately: technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule. 'Technically feasible' is not the same as 'approved'.

Marginal economics needs a decision, not a vague answer. State the payback, the net benefit after capital, and the conditions that change the result. A short payback with a legal delay is still a schedule problem.

For the fee portal, the numbers say the build is possible and the return is thin. The team should trim scope, delay SMS receipts if allowed, or negotiate a lower gateway fee. A 3-month deadline with an unapproved audit rule is a no-go until the rule is settled.
Feasibility asks whether to start. Validation asks whether the written requirements are right. Keep the two reports separate so a weak business case is not hidden inside a good requirements document.

figure.caption: Running costs and ₹2,00,000 a year of spread capital turn a ₹3,60,000 overtime saving into just ₹8,000 a year. With a payback of 2.88 years the report calls the portal marginal, so the team should start on minimum scope.

spec.title: Fee portal: economic check
spec.aria: A left-to-right chain of the fee portal's money: manual overtime ₹3,60,000 a year, less running costs ₹1,52,000, leaves a cash saving of ₹2,08,000, less capital ₹2,00,000 a year, leaving a net benefit of ₹8,000 a year and a verdict of marginal.

examples.question: A college plans an online fee portal for 8,000 students. Each student pays twice a year. Peak load is 300 payments per hour. One-time budget is ₹6,00,000 over a 3-year life. Manual overtime costs ₹150 per clerk-hour and each payment needs 9 extra clerk minutes. Portal running costs: payment gateway ₹6 per payment, SMS receipt ₹1 per payment, maintenance ₹40,000 per year. Check technical, economic, schedule, operational and legal feasibility. Use the given numbers.
steps: Peak rate: 300 payments/hour ÷ 60 minutes/hour = 5 payments/minute. A web server handles this easily, so the technical check passes.
Payments per year: 8,000 students × 2 payments/student = 16,000 payments/year.
Manual overtime: ₹150/hour ÷ 60 = ₹2.50/minute. Each payment needs 9 minutes × ₹2.50/minute = ₹22.50 per payment. Annual manual cost = 16,000 × ₹22.50 = ₹3,60,000/year.
Portal running costs: gateway 16,000 × ₹6 = ₹96,000/year; SMS 16,000 × ₹1 = ₹16,000/year; maintenance ₹40,000/year. Operating total = ₹96,000 + ₹16,000 + ₹40,000 = ₹1,52,000/year.
Annual cash saving before capital = ₹3,60,000 − ₹1,52,000 = ₹2,08,000/year. Payback = ₹6,00,000 ÷ ₹2,08,000 = 2.88 years.
Annual capital = ₹6,00,000 ÷ 3 = ₹2,00,000/year. Net annual benefit after capital = ₹2,08,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹8,000/year. Three-year net = 3 × ₹2,08,000 − ₹6,00,000 = ₹24,000.
Schedule: 3 months for login, payment gateway, receipt, reconciliation and SMS is tight. A minimum scope is login, payment, receipt and reconciliation; SMS can follow.
Operational and legal: parents need SMS receipts; payment data must follow college audit rules. Conclusion: technically feasible, economically marginal, schedule risky.
examples.answer: The portal is technically feasible at 5 payments/minute, economically marginal with payback 2.88 years and net ₹8,000/year after capital, and schedule-risky at 3 months; start only with the minimum scope and a legal/audit check.
examples.check:
students = 8000
payments_per_student = 2
peak_per_hour = 300
manual_minutes = 9
clerk_rate_per_hour = 150
gateway_fee = 6
sms_fee = 1
maintenance = 40000
one_time = 600000
life = 3

payments = students * payments_per_student
peak_per_minute = peak_per_hour / 60
clerk_rate_per_minute = clerk_rate_per_hour / 60
manual_cost_per_payment = manual_minutes * clerk_rate_per_minute
manual_cost_per_year = payments * manual_cost_per_payment
gateway_cost = payments * gateway_fee
sms_cost = payments * sms_fee
operating_cost = gateway_cost + sms_cost + maintenance
cash_saving = manual_cost_per_year - operating_cost
payback = one_time / cash_saving
capital_per_year = one_time / life
net_annual = cash_saving - capital_per_year
three_year_net = cash_saving * life - one_time

print(float(peak_per_minute))
print(float(payments))
print(float(manual_cost_per_payment))
print(float(manual_cost_per_year))
print(float(operating_cost))
print(float(cash_saving))
print(round(payback, 2))
print(float(capital_per_year))
print(float(net_annual))
print(float(three_year_net))

traps: Feasibility is only money. Technical, legal, operational and schedule checks can each stop a project.
Using peak load as average load. A portal that handles average traffic can fail at the fee-deadline hour.
Calling feasibility validation. Feasibility asks whether to start; validation asks whether the written requirements are right.
Forgetting running costs. Gateway fees, SMS and support can erase clerk overtime savings.
Treating the budget as an annual cost. A one-time ₹6,00,000 over 3 years is ₹2,00,000/year.

quiz.q: List the five checks in a feasibility study.
quiz.a: Technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule feasibility.

quiz.q: Why is the requirements engineering process drawn as a loop?
quiz.a: Validation can find missing or wrong requirements, sending work back to elicitation or analysis. Management runs throughout and keeps changes visible.

quiz.q: A system must handle 240 payments per hour. What is the rate per minute?
A portal costs ₹4,00,000 with a 2-year life. It saves ₹90,000/year before running costs; running costs are ₹30,000/year. Find annual capital cost, net annual benefit, and judge the economic case.
quiz.a: Annual capital = ₹4,00,000 ÷ 2 = ₹2,00,000/year. Cash saving = ₹90,000 − ₹30,000 = ₹60,000/year. Net annual benefit = ₹60,000 − ₹2,00,000 = −₹1,40,000/year. The economic case is weak; savings must rise or costs must fall.

quiz.q: Manual fee collection costs ₹2,40,000/year. Portal operating costs are ₹80,000/year and one-time cost is ₹4,80,000 over 3 years. Find annual net benefit after annualizing capital.
quiz.a: Annual capital = ₹4,80,000 ÷ 3 = ₹1,60,000/year. Total annual cost = ₹80,000 + ₹1,60,000 = ₹2,40,000/year. Net annual benefit = ₹2,40,000 − ₹2,40,000 = ₹0/year, so it breaks even.

quiz.q: Why is a feasibility study not a full business case?
quiz.a: It is a short screen with measured checks. A full business case compares alternatives, forecasts cash flows and covers funding decisions in more detail.

quiz.q: What is one output of requirements validation?
quiz.a: Review records, testable acceptance checks or defect reports sent back for correction.

quiz.q: A project passes technical and economic checks but needs a legal approval that takes 4 months, while delivery is 3 months. What should the feasibility report say?
quiz.a: The project is not go as planned. Legal and schedule checks fail. Delay delivery, reduce scope, or obtain the approval before committing.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, feasibility appears as a short discovery phase with a technical spike, a cost model and a compliance checklist. Teams also add security, privacy, accessibility and vendor-lock-in checks. Product managers keep a lightweight business case beside the feasibility note.
